name: Sihanouk International Airport
before:
Cambodia's third international airport, 20 km east of Sihanoukville and the way in for the southern coast and islands. It is named, like the province, after King Norodom Sihanouk, and is also known as Kang Keng. The code KOS comes from Kampong Som, the town's other name.

The runway is 3,300 metres and takes large aircraft, with five stands and a full set of navigation aids. Rescue and firefighting cover is at ICAO category 5.

Its history has been stop and start. The airfield was built in the 1960s with Soviet help, then lay dormant through the Khmer Rouge years and long after. It formally reopened in January 2007 with a lengthened runway and widened taxiways, but scheduled flights stopped again after an accident that June and did not return until December 2011, when Cambodia Angkor Air began flying from Siem Reap. A triangle route linking Siem Reap, Sihanoukville and Phnom Penh followed in 2013.
after:
Sihanoukville's airport, 20 km east of the city and the way in for the coast and islands. The runway is 3,300 metres and takes large aircraft.

In late September 2026 the airport's departures board showed flights to Siem Reap and Ho Chi Minh City with Air Cambodia, to Kuala Lumpur with AirAsia and to Kunming with Ruili Airlines. Routes change, so check the current schedule before booking.

claims.claim: 20 km east of the city
claims.note: The operator's live page says 20 km south east of the city centre and Wikipedia 20 km east. The straight line is 12.0 km (ratio 1.67, just over the 1.6 allowance), so under the method the figure needs a second written source, and it has one: the operator. The 20 km is best read as the road distance; an airport-coordination profile from about 2009 (its traffic tables run 2006 to 2008) gives 12 km, which is the straight line. The bearing (111 degrees) is east, and south east is also within the allowance.

claims.note: The operator's release of October 2020 marks the completion of the runway's extension to 3,300 metres from 2,500, for Code E aircraft such as the Boeing 777-300ER and Airbus A350-1000; its masterplan release of June 2020 says the same. Wikipedia gives 3,300 metres for 4E aircraft but dates the extension to the 2007 reopening, which the operator contradicts (see the cut below).

claims.note: Replaces the route history, which stopped in 2013 (Cambodia Angkor Air from Siem Reap in December 2011, the Siem Reap, Sihanoukville and Phnom Penh triangle in 2013; both cut below). Attributed to the airport's own live board, read on 24 September 2026, which covers 24 to 26 September: Air Cambodia K6 130 to Siem Reap (SAI) and K6 838 to Ho Chi Minh (SGN); AirAsia Cambodia KT 175 and AirAsia AK 265 to Kuala Lumpur; Ruili Airlines DR 5030 to Kunming. No Phnom Penh flight appears. The airport's destination page (saved as op-destinations) lists Siem Reap, Wuxi, Kuala Lumpur, Bangkok and Ho Chi Minh, and its airline page (op-airlines, titled 'Test') names more airlines, so the text rests on the board alone, as an attributed statement, and says which days it covers. AKP (21 January 2026) reports a Cambodia Airways route to Chengdu three times a week from that day; it is not on this week's board (held back below). Review (24 Sep): 'For 24 to 26 September 2026' became 'In late September 2026' (the board was read on 24 September and covered the 24th to the 26th), and a line of advice follows it, so the snapshot does not read as a timetable.

claims.claim: Cambodia's third international airport
claims.why: A ranking that no current source gives. The operator called Cambodia's international airports a network of three in 2020, with Sihanoukville far behind Phnom Penh and Siem Reap (1.6 million passengers in 2019, against 6 million and 3.9 million). Since then both larger airports have moved: Siem Reap's to a new airport (Cambodia Airports' concession there ended on 15 October 2023) and Phnom Penh's to Techo (9 September 2025). VINCI's 2025 table covers only Techo and Sihanoukville, and no saved page lists Cambodia's international airports today.

claims.claim: Held back: passenger traffic, 172,000 in 2025 against 1.6 million in 2019
claims.why: Held back: the old text gives no passenger figure, so under the like-for-like rule this stays out. VINCI's table for 2025 (published 20 January 2026) gives Sihanoukville 172,000 passengers (up 84 per cent) and 2,669 aircraft movements (up 29 per cent); Wikipedia's infobox gives the same, citing VINCI. The operator's 2020 releases put 2019 at more than 1.6 million, after 94,000 in 2015 and 338,000 in 2017. So traffic is about a tenth of its 2019 level. VINCI owns 70 per cent of Cambodia Airports, so the two are one group: this would go in as 'on VINCI Airports' figures'.

claims.claim: Held back: FCDO advice for Cambodia
claims.why: Held back: warnings that replace nothing. The FCDO (updated 19 March 2026, still current 24 September 2026) advises against all but essential travel within 20 km of the land border with Thailand, after heavy fighting in 2025 and a ceasefire signed on 27 December, with land crossings still suspended; Sihanoukville is not in that area. Its safety page warns that tourist boats sometimes run despite weather warnings, particularly between Sihanoukville and the nearby islands, lists Sihanoukville's beaches and nearby islands among petty-crime hotspots, and says job-scam gangs hold trafficking victims in compounds in and around Sihanoukville. The boat warning is the one an agent sending clients to the islands might want, as an attributed sentence.
